passage: Two stories are commonly told about the measures that late medieval and early modern cities took against plague. In the first, the health boards of the Italian city-states, with their isolation hospitals, their passes for travellers and their periods of enforced seclusion for ships and households, are the ancestors of modern public health: rational officials confronting an epidemic with the tools of an emerging state. In the second, the same measures are a chapter in the history of coercion, in which the sick and the poor were locked away, their goods burned and their livelihoods destroyed by authorities who feared contagion more than they valued the people who might carry it. Each story can be furnished with abundant evidence. What both tend to overlook is that the measures could work only with a degree of cooperation that neither officials nor force could guarantee.

Quarantine depends, at its most basic, on information. A household must be shut up before the disease spreads from it, which means that someone must report the first case, and the people best placed to report it are the members of the household themselves, together with their neighbours. Every one of them had reasons to stay silent. A shut household lost its income; its members might be removed to an isolation hospital from which many did not return; its bedding and clothing might be burned. Families that concealed a death, bribed an inspector or slipped out of the city before the doors were sealed were not simply defying authority. They were responding sensibly to the costs that reporting imposed on them, and neighbours who might have informed on them faced, in their turn, the prospect of being shut up beside them.

Where the measures had any success, it seems to have been because authorities, sometimes reluctantly, took on obligations in return. Some cities fed shut-up households at public expense, paid compensation for goods that had been destroyed, or relied on clergy and charitable brotherhoods to bring food, relief and reassurance to the confined. Such provisions were expensive and often inadequate, and the surviving records do not allow us to say with any confidence how much difference they made to mortality. But they changed the calculation facing a family that suspected illness, and the complaints of officials who lacked the means to provide them suggest that concealment rose when relief failed.

It might be objected that this underrates force. Cities did post guards, punish concealment severely and, on occasion, execute those who broke quarantine. Yet harshness had a cost that its advocates rarely counted: the more frightening the consequences of discovery, the stronger the incentive not to be discovered, and an epidemic that goes underground is harder, not easier, to contain. A household that expected to be sealed in with its sick, guarded and fined had every reason to wait, to hide the first symptoms and to hope, and each day of waiting was a day in which the disease could travel. Severity could secure compliance from those already known to the authorities; it could not make the unknown come forward.

The lesson is not that plague regulations were humane, for many plainly were not, nor that they were futile. It is that measures which depend on people revealing something about themselves are bargains, whether or not those who impose them think of them in that way, and the point is not confined to plague. Their success is limited by what disclosure costs the person who discloses, and an authority that wishes to know must first make knowing bearable.

passage: Few school subjects have lost their defenders as quickly as handwriting. When most adult writing passes through a keyboard or a touchscreen, the hours once devoted to forming letters on lined paper can look like a ritual preserved out of institutional habit rather than educational necessity. Why, the argument runs, should a child labour over the loops of a joined script that she will rarely use after leaving school, when the same time could be given to typing, programming or simply reading more widely? The objection has the considerable appeal of common sense, and part of it is right. But it rests on a narrow idea of what handwriting lessons were ever for.

The narrow idea treats handwriting as a delivery system, a way of getting words from a head onto a surface, and judged by that standard alone it has plainly been outpaced. Yet for a young child, forming a letter by hand is also a way of learning the letter. To write a b rather than a d, the child must attend to direction, proportion and the small differences that distinguish one shape from its neighbours, and that sustained attention seems to help fix the shapes in memory in a way that pressing a key does not. A keyboard presents every letter ready-made; the hand has to build each one. Several researchers have suggested that this building is part of how early readers come to recognise letters at all, though the evidence is still being argued over and is far from settled.

There is a second, quieter benefit, which concerns older students rather than beginners. Students who take notes by hand cannot transcribe a lecture word for word, because the hand is too slow. They are forced to choose, compress and rephrase, and that compression is itself a kind of thinking, an early and private interpretation of what the lecturer actually argued. The student with a laptop can capture far more, and may understand far less, since verbatim copying can proceed without the words ever being weighed. The slowness that makes handwriting look obsolete is, in this setting, precisely its use.

None of this is an argument for preserving every feature of the old curriculum. The insistence on one elegant joined style, and the marks lost for an untidy loop, had more to do with the manners of an earlier age than with learning, and they can be abandoned without much loss. Nor should typing be neglected in the name of tradition; children need both. The case for handwriting, properly made, is modest: not that it is beautiful or traditional, but that the hand teaches the eye and slows the mind in ways that are useful precisely because they are inefficient. A curriculum that drops it to save time may find that it has saved the wrong thing.

passage: When a child falls into a disused well or a group of miners is trapped underground, communities will spend almost without limit to bring them out. Engineers are flown in, machines are diverted from other work, and no one asks whether the money might have been better used. The same communities, meanwhile, routinely decline measures that would save far more lives at far lower cost: safer road junctions, better lighting on rural highways, routine screening for common diseases. To many economists and policy analysts, the contrast is simply an error. A life saved by a guardrail is no less a life than one saved by a rescue shaft; that we cannot name the person in advance makes no difference to the value of what is saved. On this view the preference for identified over statistical lives is a bias, and a costly one, to be corrected by accounting that treats every life saved alike.

Much of this critique seems to me correct. The people whose deaths a guardrail prevents are not abstractions; they are as real as the trapped miners, and they would have suffered and been mourned in the same way. If we spend a hundred times more per life on rescue than on prevention, a great many people die who need not have, and the fact that we never learn their names does not make their deaths any less our doing. It is worth noticing, too, that the identified lives we rush to save are often identified by chance: they are the victims whose plight happens to be reported, while others in similar danger elsewhere receive nothing, because no one is watching.

Yet the critique moves too quickly when it concludes that the impulse to rescue has no rational content. What a community expresses when it refuses to abandon a known person in peril is a commitment that has value beyond the life in question: an assurance, to everyone, that if they are ever in that position they will not be left to die because the arithmetic was unfavourable. This assurance is a real good, and it is one that statistical accounting, which counts only lives saved, has no column for. It is enjoyed by people who are never in danger, and it shapes how the members of a community regard one another.

Nor need this good conflict with the analyst's preferred standpoint. The strongest case for prevention is made from the position of someone who does not yet know whether he will be a victim: from there, each of us would prefer the policy that most improves our own chances, and that is usually prevention. But someone in that position would also want the assurance that rescue provides, and would be willing to pay something for it. Properly understood, then, the choice made under that uncertainty is not between rescue and prevention but about the proportion in which to buy them, and it is hard to believe that the proportion would resemble our present spending, in which prevention is starved while rescue is limitless.

The lesson is not that rescue should be abandoned in the name of consistency, a policy that would purchase a few more statistical lives at the price of a community in which no one could count on being saved. It is that the scandal lies on the other side of the ledger. We do not rescue too much; we prevent too little, and the impulse to rescue, rightly valued, gives no excuse for that neglect.

passage: Tourists, it is often observed, are rarely content with what is shown to them. The monument, the parade, the dance performed on a stage in the hotel courtyard: all of these are understood to be presentations, arranged for visitors, and for that reason they seem to many travellers less real than whatever lies behind them. What the discerning visitor wants is the back region, the kitchen rather than the dining room, the village household rather than the folk show, the place where people are simply living rather than performing. Tourism, on this view, is a search for the unperformed, conducted by people whose very presence makes performance likely.

The difficulty is that the search creates its object, for once visitors will pay to see behind the scenes, behind the scenes becomes a scene. Homestays are furnished to look lived in; working kitchens are tidied and lit for the guided tour; a weaving cooperative arranges its looms so that visitors can watch the ordinary work of the day at a convenient hour. Each of these presents itself as a glimpse of the back, and each is in fact another front, built in the shape of a back. Critics of tourism have made much of this, arguing that the visitor who congratulates himself on having escaped the tourist trail has merely been led down a more expensive branch of it.

The criticism is accurate about the arrangements and, I think, mistaken about the tourists. It assumes that they are dupes who believe they have found the real thing and would be dismayed to learn otherwise. Many are nothing of the kind: asked directly, a good number will say that of course the homestay was prepared for them, that of course the cooperative works differently when no one is watching. What they value is not the illusion of having seen the unstaged but the experience of being admitted, of being received as a guest rather than seated as a spectator, and that experience is not falsified by the knowledge that it was arranged. A theatre audience is not deceived merely because it knows the actors are acting.

If there is a cost in all this, it falls elsewhere. Every back region that is opened to visitors must be replaced by another, further back, where the hosts can live without being watched, and in places where tourism is the main source of income, that retreat can go a long way. The family that rents out its courtyard confines its own life to a back room; the village that stages its festival for visitors holds the version that matters to it in the off season, or not at all. The more successfully a community sells access to its private life, the less private life it has left to sell, and the less it has left to keep for itself.

The usual question about staged authenticity is whether the tourist is being cheated. That question flatters the tourist by placing his experience at the centre of the moral picture, and it is in any case usually answered in his favour, since he generally receives what he knowingly pays for. The harder question concerns the hosts, and it is not whether they are deceiving anyone but how much of their lives they can afford to keep out of view. A tourism that respected its hosts would measure itself not by how much it manages to reveal but by how much it is content to leave alone.

passage: In a society whose members hold different and often incompatible views about the meaning of life and the sources of value, on what basis may some of them use the power of the state to make others comply with laws? One influential answer holds that coercive laws must be justifiable by reasons that all reasonable citizens could accept, whatever their wider convictions. A law defended solely by appeal to a doctrine that many of one's fellow citizens reject, whether that doctrine is religious or secular, treats them as subjects to be managed rather than as equals to be persuaded. The requirement to offer such shared, or public, reasons is usually called the ideal of public reason.

Critics have objected that the ideal asks too much of ordinary citizens. People do not keep their deepest convictions in a compartment separate from their political views; for many, their sense of what justice requires flows directly from a philosophical or religious outlook. To tell such citizens that they may vote, campaign and argue only on grounds detachable from that outlook is to ask them to enter public life as strangers to themselves. Worse, the demand seems to fall unevenly, since those whose convictions already happen to resemble the shared vocabulary are asked to give up nothing.

Much of this objection depends on reading the ideal as a rule about what citizens may say. It is more plausible to read it as a test that laws must pass. On this reading a citizen may give whatever reasons move her, in the street, in the press or in the voting booth, and the ideal is satisfied so long as the law that is eventually enacted can also be supported by reasons that do not depend on any one contested doctrine. The burden then falls most heavily on those who exercise official power, on legislators drafting statutes and judges explaining decisions, rather than on citizens in conversation with one another.

This reading does not remove every difficulty. If a citizen offers public reasons she does not herself find convincing, merely because she knows they are the only reasons that will count, her contribution begins to look less like persuasion and more like strategy. The ideal was meant to express respect for others as fellow reasoners, and insincere argument is a poor vehicle for respect. But this worry, though real, tells against a particular style of advocacy rather than against the test itself. A law can be justified in shared terms even if some of its supporters were moved by other considerations, just as a bridge can be sound though some of those who voted to build it understood nothing of engineering.

passage: For a long time emotions were cast as the adversaries of reason, surges of feeling that cloud judgement and must be governed by it. A more recent and considerably more flattering view inverts this picture. Emotions, it holds, are themselves judgements, or are at least constructed around them. To be afraid of a dog is to judge that the dog is dangerous; to feel indignant is to regard oneself as having been treated unjustly. The view has an obvious appeal. It explains why emotions can be appropriate or inappropriate to their circumstances, why we can sometimes argue a friend out of her jealousy by showing her that she has misread a situation, and why emotions are directed at objects rather than being mere sensations, like an itch or a cramp, that are about nothing at all.

The difficulty arises from emotions that persist against judgement. A traveller may know perfectly well that flying is far safer than the drive to the airport, may say so and sincerely believe it, and still grip the armrest in terror as the aircraft climbs. If fear were a judgement that flying is dangerous, the traveller would be simultaneously affirming and denying the same proposition, and her condition would be a straightforward contradiction. Yet it does not feel like a contradiction, nor do we treat it as one; we recognise it as a familiar kind of inner conflict, unpleasant but not absurd.

A better model is perception. When two lines of equal length are drawn with arrowheads pointing in opposite directions, one continues to look longer even after a ruler has shown that they are equal. Seeing is not believing, so the conflict involves no contradiction. Emotions, on this model, are something like perceptions of value: fear presents the climbing aircraft as dangerous in the way the illusion presents one line as longer. Such presentations are usually reliable and usually agree with our considered views, which is why the judgement theory seemed so plausible. When they disagree, we have the emotional counterpart of an optical illusion.

The analogy should not be pressed too far. We do not blame anyone for seeing the lines as unequal, but we do sometimes criticise people for their fears and resentments, and we expect them to work on them. This suggests that emotions, unlike most perceptions, are partly answerable to the person who has them: they can be reshaped over time through reflection and repeated experience, even if they cannot be dismissed by a single act of judgement. The perceptual model explains why emotional conflict is not contradiction; it must be supplemented to explain why it is nevertheless an occasion for responsibility.

passage: The familiar story of urbanisation runs in one direction. People leave the countryside for the city, struggle for a generation in its least desirable quarters, and are eventually absorbed, their children speaking the city's idiom and regarding the village as a place of grandparents and holidays. Migration, on this account, is a passage with a beginning and an end, and the only question worth asking about a migrant is how far along it he has come. The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries. But it has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting, and this has made it difficult to see a pattern that is, in much of the world, at least as common.

A large number of those who work in cities never complete the journey the story describes. They come for a season of construction or a few years in a factory, return for the harvest, a wedding or an illness in the family, and come back again, sometimes to the same city and sometimes to another. Their earnings pay school fees and debts in the village; the village holds their land, their elders and, often, their spouses and children. A household can live this way for decades, and many do. Seen through the one-way story, such people are migrants who have not yet settled, a transitional population whose double life is a symptom of incomplete integration. Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains.

The distinction matters because city governments have tended to act on the first reading. A resident whose household is registered elsewhere, whose stay is irregular, and whose address is a worksite or a shared rented room is easily treated as a visitor: excluded from subsidised housing, from schools for the children who come along, from the electoral roll, and from the attention of politicians who answer to those who are on it. The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged.

It would be a mistake to romanticise circulation in its turn. Some who move back and forth would settle in the city if they could, and return to the village only because the city offers them nothing to stay for; for them, circularity is less a strategy than a sentence. Others genuinely prefer a life lived in two places and would keep it even if the city were more welcoming. The difficulty is that from the outside the two groups look identical, and a policy designed for one will misjudge the other.

What follows is not a single programme but a change in the condition attached to belonging. A city that made its entitlements portable, that allowed a worker to enrol his children in school without proving permanent residence, and that encouraged cheap rental housing suited to stays of months rather than decades would serve both groups at once. It would allow those who wish to settle to do so, and those who wish to circulate to circulate without penalty. What it would cease to do is demand that a person surrender one home as the price of being recognised in another.

passage: A common modern objection to traditional mourning customs is that they put grief on a timetable. Many traditions mark fixed days after a death, often a gathering within the first two weeks, another around the fortieth day and a final observance at the first anniversary, and for centuries some communities prescribed the clothes a widow might wear and the months during which she should not appear at celebrations. To a sensibility that prizes authentic feeling, this looks like an intrusion: grief, it is said, is personal, it follows no calendar, and nobody has the right to tell a bereaved person when to stop.

The objection contains a truth, but it misreads what the calendar was for. The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts. What they did was settle a set of practical questions that otherwise fall, at the worst possible moment, on the people least able to answer them. When should relatives visit, and when should they leave? What is it acceptable to say? When may the household resume ordinary work without seeming callous? A prescribed sequence answers all of these in advance, so that the bereaved are spared the labour of inventing their own conduct while they are exhausted, and so that neighbours know when their presence is expected.

In this sense the timetable was addressed less to the mourner than to everyone around the mourner, translating an event that isolates one household into a sequence of obligations that the wider community could recognise and discharge. Its main work was coordination. Where such scripts have weakened, the result has not obviously been freer grief. Friends hesitate, unsure whether a call would comfort or intrude; colleagues say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing; and the bereaved, told that they may grieve in their own way, often find that their own way is a lonely one, because nobody else knows what part to play in it.

This is not an argument for restoring every old rule, nor for pretending that the old forms were uniformly benign. Some customs plainly bore down hardest on those with least power, and a widow who was obliged to wear mourning for years was being policed as much as consoled. The lesson is narrower. A society that abandons shared forms for mourning does not thereby hand grief back to the individual; it removes the cues that let others accompany it. Any replacement worth having would keep that coordinating function while dropping the demand that inner feeling match an outward schedule.

passage: Few technical metaphors have succeeded as completely as the cloud. To store files 'in the cloud' is to imagine them floating somewhere overhead, available from anywhere, belonging to no place in particular and weighing nothing at all. The image is not simply wrong; from the point of view of a user, it describes the experience rather well. A photograph taken on a phone appears on a laptop moments later, and the user neither knows nor needs to know where it has been in between. Yet the metaphor has migrated from describing an experience to shaping how whole societies think about a vast industrial system, and in that second role it misleads.

What sits behind the cloud is emphatically material. It consists of large buildings filled with servers, which consume great quantities of electricity and must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies; of cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines; of particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground. Each of these is somewhere, and being somewhere means being subject to the laws of a particular state, to the weather and geology of a particular region, and to the politics of the towns asked to host the buildings and supply their power. A data centre can strain a local grid or compete with farms for water, and a damaged cable can slow communication across a region.

The metaphor makes all of this hard to see. A cloud has no address, so questions about which country's courts can demand access to stored data come to seem technical rather than political. A cloud uses nothing, so the energy cost of keeping old files indefinitely available is easy to forget. And a cloud is diffuse, which suggests resilience, whereas in practice a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward with surprising speed.

Defenders of the metaphor might point out that hiding complexity is precisely what good computing does. Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message, and abstractions of this kind are why ordinary people can use powerful systems at all. That is true, but it confuses two audiences. Abstraction is a gift to the user at the moment of use; it becomes a liability when it is carried over into the deliberations of citizens, regulators and planners, whose task is precisely to decide where the buildings go, who supplies their power and whose laws govern what they hold. For them, the useful question is not where the cloud is but how it came to seem to be nowhere.

passage: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route.

The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument.

Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise.

The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.

passage: In the large households of the nineteenth century, the best servant was the one who was least noticed. Grand houses were built with back staircases so that maids carrying coal or slops need never meet the family on the main stairs, and bells rang in a basement corridor so that a summons could be issued without anyone having to see who answered it. In some houses servants were expected to turn aside, even to face the wall, when a member of the family passed. It is tempting to read all this as snobbery, a taste for keeping inferiors out of sight, but snobbery explains less than it seems to. The invisibility of servants was not a by-product of the genteel household; it was one of the things the household was for.

What a gentleman's house displayed, above all, was ease: meals that appeared, fires that were lit, linen that was clean, all without visible effort. The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed. A servant glimpsed scrubbing a step was a reminder that comfort had a cost and a source; a servant unseen allowed the family to experience comfort as a natural condition of their kind of life. In this sense the architecture of concealment did not merely reflect a social hierarchy but helped to produce one, by allowing one class to appear exempt from necessity.

Large-scale domestic service of this kind has largely disappeared, and it is easy to assume that its logic went with it. Yet much of the modern service economy seems designed to recreate the same experience by other means. Food arrives at the door from a kitchen the customer never sees, carried by a courier who is a first name on a screen. Offices are cleaned at night, after the staff have gone home. Apps promise that groceries, laundry and repairs will simply happen, and their designers speak, revealingly, of removing friction, as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work.

The comparison must not be pressed too far. The modern courier or cleaner is not bound to a single household, keeps hours that end, and has legal protections that a Victorian scullery maid lacked; to call such workers servants is to erase real gains. But the aspiration that the old houses expressed in brick and bells, the wish to receive service without meeting the server, has proved remarkably durable. What has changed is less the wish than the means of satisfying it, and the means are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase.

passage: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate.

There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there.

The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational.

If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.

passage: In the design of a clinical trial, the placebo plays the role of nothing. Patients in one group receive the drug, patients in the other receive an inert imitation, and whatever improvement the second group shows is subtracted from the first as background noise. The logic is sound for its purpose, which is to establish whether a molecule does anything beyond the act of being given. But the habit of treating the placebo arm as a measure of nothing has encouraged a further and less defensible assumption, that the improvement seen there is not real, or at least not interesting.

It is both. What patients in a placebo group respond to is not the sugar in the pill but everything that surrounds it: the consultation, the explanation, the expectation of relief, the ritual of taking something at set hours, the attention of people whose job is to help. Some researchers prefer to speak of a 'meaning response' for this reason, since the inert pill is merely the occasion on which the meaning of being treated is delivered. On this view the placebo arm is not a blank but a measurement of how much the context of care can do by itself.

The standard objection to using such effects deliberately has been ethical. A placebo, it was assumed, works only if the patient is deceived, and deceiving patients violates the trust on which medicine depends. Several small trials have unsettled this assumption by giving patients pills that were openly described as inert and still recording improvements in symptoms that the patients reported themselves. The findings are preliminary, and it is not clear how much of the effect survives once the novelty of an unusual study wears off. Even so, they suggest that deception may be less essential to the response than was believed, and that the ritual may matter more than the belief that the pill is active.

Enthusiasts are quick to go further than the evidence allows. Responses to placebo are most consistent for symptoms that are experienced and reported, such as pain, nausea and fatigue; there is little reason to think that the meaning of a consultation can shrink a tumour or clear an infection. The more useful conclusion is not that doctors should prescribe sugar pills but that the manner of care is itself a part of treatment. A health system that shortens consultations to save money may be removing an active ingredient without ever recording the loss, because its effect was always filed under nothing.

passage: When information was scarce, the economic problem it posed was one of supply: how to print, carry and store enough of it for the people who wanted it. That problem has largely been solved, and its solution has exposed another. The abundance of material has made scarce the one resource that every piece of it requires, namely the attention of those who are meant to receive it. Every article, message and video competes for the same limited hours of the same limited minds, and while the cost of producing one more piece of content has fallen almost to nothing, the supply of attention has not grown at all.

This shift explains a feature of modern commerce that once seemed puzzling, the enormous number of services offered at no charge. A search engine, a social network or a mobile game that costs its user nothing is not a gift; it is paid for with attention, which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers, so that the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded. Described in this way, the arrangement is not obviously unfair. Many people would gladly exchange a few seconds of distraction for a useful map or a convenient way of keeping in touch with distant friends, and for them the bargain may be a good one.

The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the fact that the price is never stated. When a product is sold for money, its price is a number that buyers can compare across sellers, and the comparison disciplines firms, since a shop that charges too much loses its customers to a cheaper rival. Attention has no such number attached to it. A user cannot easily tell whether one free application takes ten minutes of her day or two hours, still less whether a rival would take less, and so the competitive pressure that keeps money prices in check operates feebly, if at all. Firms competing for attention are therefore rewarded not for charging less of it but for extracting more, and the design of their products follows accordingly, towards endless feeds, automatic playback and notifications timed to recapture a wandering mind.

It does not follow that free services should be prohibited or that their users are dupes. What follows is narrower and, in a way, more practical: a market in which one side cannot see the price it pays will not protect that side as markets ordinarily do, and remedies should therefore aim at making the price visible. A service that reported to each user, plainly and regularly, how much time it had absorbed would not end the trade in attention, but it would give its users what every functioning market requires, a figure to compare.

passage: A persistent habit of literary talk treats the short story as a smaller novel: the same materials of character, setting and incident, simply supplied in lesser quantities. On this view the story is where writers practise before attempting the larger form, and a collection of stories is a kind of portfolio of novels not yet written. The habit is reinforced by publishers, who have long regarded collections as harder to sell, and by critics who praise a story for being 'as rich as a novel', as though richness of that kind were the measure of success. Prizes and anthologies have sometimes followed suit, treating a writer's stories as preparation and the first novel as the real debut.

The comparison misunderstands where a short story does its work. A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change. A story has no such time to spend. What it has instead is selection, and selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself. When a story shows a woman packing a suitcase, pausing over a single photograph and putting it back in the drawer, the eleven years of marriage that the story never describes are present precisely because they are withheld. The reader does not receive them; she supplies them, and the supplying is the experience.

This is why expanding a fine story so rarely improves it. Give the woman a history, a sister to confide in, a chapter on the courtship, and the photograph becomes one detail among many rather than the point on which everything turns. The gaps that had been doing the work are filled with information, and information, however well written, is less charged than implication. The reader who had been supplying the marriage is now simply told about it, and being told is a lesser kind of participation. The story's brevity was not a limitation it laboured under but the condition of its force.

None of this means that stories and novels never meet. Some writers have plainly used stories as sketches, and more than one long novel began as a few pages its author could not leave alone. Nor is brevity a virtue in itself; a weak story can hide behind its shortness, gesturing at depths it has not earned. The claim is narrower: that when a story succeeds on its own terms, it succeeds by a method the novel mostly cannot use, and that judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions.

passage: A scientific paper presents itself as a complete set of instructions. Its methods section lists the materials, the quantities, the temperatures and the timings, and the implicit promise is that anyone competent who follows them will see what the authors saw. This promise underwrites one of the most cherished ideas about science: that its knowledge is public, available in principle to anyone who can read, and independent of the particular people who first produced it. When a laboratory fails to reproduce a published result, the natural suspicion therefore falls either on the original claim or on the care of the people who tried to repeat it.

Anyone who has worked at a laboratory bench knows that the promise is only partly kept. Many techniques depend on skills that their practitioners cannot fully articulate: how firmly to tap a tube, how long a mixture should look cloudy before it is ready, which faint smudge on an image is signal and which is dirt. Such knowledge is not secret, and it is not mystical. It is simply of a kind that is acquired by doing and by watching others do, in the way that one learns to ride a bicycle rather than the way one learns a telephone number. A methods section can point toward it, but it cannot transmit it, any more than a manual can make its reader a competent cyclist.

It is not unusual for a group trying to build a new kind of instrument from published descriptions alone to fail again and again, while another group that has sent a member to spend some weeks in the original laboratory, or has received a visitor from it, succeeds, often without being able to say afterwards what the crucial difference was. In such cases the written instructions were not wrong. They were incomplete in ways that neither their authors nor their readers could have specified in advance, because the authors did not know which of the many things they did without thinking were the things that mattered.

Recognising this does not license complacency about how methods are reported. A great deal that is now left out of papers could be written down, and the habit of omitting it, whether to save space or to protect an advantage, deserves the criticism it receives. But the recognition does alter what we should expect from reform. Demanding ever longer methods sections will capture the explicit portion of a technique more fully while leaving the tacit portion exactly where it was. If the goal is that results can be checked by people other than those who produced them, some of the effort now spent on documents might be better spent on movement: on funding researchers to visit one another's laboratories, on recording procedures as they are actually performed, and on treating the training of a replicator as part of the cost of a replication.

There is a larger consequence as well. The picture of scientific knowledge as a body of public statements, detachable from the people who hold it, turns out to be an idealisation. Much of what a field knows lives in the hands of its practitioners and moves only when they do. This is not a reason to distrust that knowledge, since skills can be tested by their results as surely as statements can. It is a reason to treat the communities that carry it, and the slow work of passing it on, as part of the infrastructure of science rather than as a private matter of training.

passage: A familiar way of thinking about Western art music divides the creative labour with reassuring neatness. The composer makes the work and records it in a score; the performer's task is to realise the score faithfully, adding as little of himself as the music allows. On this view the score is the work, or at least its complete specification, and a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains. Its attractions are considerable. It accounts for our confidence that two strikingly different performances are nevertheless performances of the same composition, and it furnishes the critic with a standard: the performer who alters the notes has made a mistake, whatever the result sounds like.

The difficulty is that notation specifies far less than the view requires. A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less, but a great deal of what listeners hear as the character of a performance is left open or indicated only roughly. A marking that asks for a loud passage does not say how loud, and the right loudness in a small room is not the right loudness in a large hall. A word indicating a lively tempo admits a range of speeds wide enough to make one performance sound urgent and another relaxed. Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase, or how to weigh the notes of a chord against one another. These are not trivial details that a faithful performer can safely settle at random; they are much of what makes the music sound the way it does.

One response is to swing to the opposite extreme and say that the work simply is the performance, the score being no more than a set of instructions that each performer completes as she pleases. This rescues the performer's creative contribution, but at a considerable theoretical price. It cannot explain why some performances strike informed listeners as wrong-headed even when every note is in place, or why a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed has done something worse than make an unusual choice. If the score were merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements, and yet musicians make them constantly and with considerable agreement.

That agreement points to what both positions conspicuously omit. Scores are never interpreted in isolation. They are read by musicians trained in a practice: a shared and largely unwritten understanding of what the marks mean in a given style, which conventions apply, what kinds of freedom are expected and where those freedoms stop. In music of one period a trill is understood to begin on the note above; in another it begins on the main note; the score is usually silent on the point, and the practice supplies the answer. The work, on this account, is neither the marks alone nor whatever a given performance makes of them, but the marks as a practice reads them. Fidelity is owed to that combination.

It may be objected that practices evolve, so that the work would apparently evolve with them, which seems absurd. But the objection establishes considerably less than it appears to. Practices do change, slowly, and the identity of a work is correspondingly less fixed than the first view supposed; that is a cost worth accepting, since it matches how musicians actually argue about performances. What does not follow is that anything goes. A practice at any moment draws lines that its members can defend, and a performer who knowingly crosses them is making a claim that must be argued for, not exercising a right.

passage: We tend to assume that each of us has a special and nearly infallible access to our own minds. Others must infer what I think and feel from my speech and behaviour, whereas I, it seems, am acquainted with my own mental states directly, without any need for inference or interpretation. For some states the assumption is plausible. If I sincerely report a sharp pain in my knee, it is hard to see what better evidence anyone could have, including me, about whether the pain is there. But the assumption is usually extended, without much reflection, to a quite different class of facts: the facts about why I did what I did.

Here the case for special access is far weaker. Imagine a shopper who chooses one of several identical scarves laid out in a row and who, asked why, cites the richer colour or the finer weave of the one she took. Since the scarves really are identical, her explanation cannot be true, yet it is offered sincerely and without hesitation. What she supplies is not a report of a cause she observed operating within her but a plausible reconstruction, drawn from a shared and largely unexamined theory of human motivation, of the kind anyone might give of why a person would choose a scarf. An onlooker armed with the same commonsense theory could have produced the same explanation, and would have been no more and no less likely to be right.

It is tempting to conclude from such cases that self-knowledge is an illusion and that we stand to ourselves essentially as strangers do, but that conclusion overreaches. The shopper's error concerns the causes of a past choice, and about such causes she may well be no better placed than anyone else. But there is another kind of question about which her position is not that of an observer at all. If she is asked which scarf she will wear tomorrow, or whether she thinks scarves make a sensible gift, she does not answer by studying evidence about herself; she answers by deciding, or by considering the merits of scarves. Her authority here derives from the fact that the answer is, in part, up to her.

The lesson, then, is not that the first person has no privilege but that its privilege has been misplaced. We are poorly placed to discover, by looking inward, the forces that moved us; we are well placed to settle what we will stand by. Confusing the two invites a double error: an unearned confidence about our own motives, and an exaggerated scepticism that would deny us even the authority we exercise whenever we make up our minds.

passage: When professional scientists first began to rely on volunteers to record birds, butterflies or the timing of spring flowers, the objection most often raised was that amateurs would make mistakes. A trained ornithologist can tell two similar warblers apart by a fragment of song; a weekend walker may not know that there are two species to distinguish. Such worries were not idle, for a single confident error repeated across many records can manufacture a trend that does not exist. Data gathered by such walkers, the argument went, would be riddled with misidentifications, and conclusions drawn from it would be built on sand.

The worry was reasonable, but experience has shown it to be aimed at the lesser target. Well-run projects have learned to ask volunteers for the kinds of observation they can make reliably, such as whether any frog was heard calling at a pond on a given evening, rather than the kinds that demand years of training. Where identification is genuinely hard, volunteers can photograph what they see and leave the naming to specialists, and records that look improbable can be flagged and checked. Errors do not vanish, but when thousands of independent observations are pooled, isolated mistakes tend to be swamped by the many correct reports around them.

The more stubborn problem lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look. People record wildlife near their homes, along popular footpaths and on fine weekends, so that their records cluster wherever leisure, access and good weather happen to coincide. They visit nature reserves more often than industrial estates, and gardens more often than farmland. A map of volunteer sightings is therefore partly a map of the species and partly a map of the observers, and no amount of skill in identification will separate the two. A bird that seems to be thriving in the suburbs may simply be living where the watchers live.

This bias is harder to correct than misidentification precisely because it is invisible in any single record. Each observation may be impeccable; the distortion appears only in the pattern. Projects that take it seriously ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times, accepting fewer and less convenient records in exchange for a sample whose shape is known. Such schemes demand more of participants, and they rarely attract the crowds that open recording does. But they show that the reliability of citizen science was never really a question about the competence of amateurs. It is a question about whether the people designing a project have thought as carefully about sampling as about skill.

passage: Arguments about charity tend to divide into two camps. On one side are those who hold that money given to help others should go wherever it will do the most good, which, given the vast differences in what a sum can buy in different places, often means far from home. On the other are those who insist that we owe something special to our own: our town, our region, our country. The first camp accuses the second of parochialism dressed up as loyalty; the second accuses the first of a cold arithmetic that would dissolve every bond that makes moral life recognisable. Each has hold of something, and each, I think, misidentifies what it is.

Begin with what the defenders of local giving get right. There really are special obligations. A parent owes more to her own children than to children in general, and no plausible ethics of giving asks her to fund a stranger's schooling before her son's. We also owe more to those we have harmed, and to those with whom we share institutions that we sustain and from which we benefit, such as a school we attended or a cooperative to which we belong. These obligations do not arise from distance. They arise from relationships: from dependence, from history, from reciprocity.

The trouble is that the case for local giving usually trades on these relationships while asking for something else. The resident who prefers to give to a shelter in his own city rather than to a health programme abroad rarely stands in any special relation to the people in the shelter. He has not harmed them, does not depend on them and shares no institution with them beyond the accident of living within the same municipal boundary. What draws him is proximity, and proximity by itself has little moral force. A sick stranger in the next street does not matter more than a sick stranger in another country simply because she is closer, though I may be better placed to help her.

That last qualification points to the strongest argument for local giving, which is not about loyalty at all but about knowledge. Near home, donors can see whether their money is used well, and can withdraw it if it is not. This is a serious consideration, but it is an empirical one, and it cuts in both directions: where reliable assessments of distant programmes exist, the advantage of proximity shrinks, and where the local charity is opaque, it disappears. What remains, once relationships and knowledge are set aside, is often a preference for help whose results one can watch, a preference that is understandable but that should not be mistaken for an obligation.
